title: Emotional Qualities of VR Space
research_question: To assess the extent to which design parameters (color, brightness, texture) influenced emotional responses to virtual spaces, and to verify if real-world affective space creation could be replicated in a simulated environment.

participants.description: 29 participants (91%) aged 18-40 (Mean=27, SD=4.8), 3 participants (9%) aged 50-76. 27 students (5 undergraduate, 13 master's, 14 doctoral/postdoctoral) and 5 professionals. 16 active (9 male/7 female), 16 inactive (8 male/8 female).
participants.recruitment: email and poster announcements on university campus at Duke University. Participation was voluntary.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A single, square living space (3.35 m x 3.35 m x 3.35 m) simulated in a 6-sided CAVE-type display (Duke DiVE). It included mixed reality elements (real chair, round table, laundry basket) and virtual furniture (study table, small bed). The space had variable design parameters: color (orange/blue), brightness (dark/light), and texture (rough/smooth).

measures.instrument: Self-report ratings on a 1-10 scale for warmth, coolness, excitement, calmness, intimacy, spaciousness, comfort.
Self-report ratings on a 1-10 scale for preference for resting and working.

mechanisms: Warm colors are known as 'advancing colors' that appear to be closer, and cool colors are known as 'receding colors' that appear to be farther away, influencing perceptions of intimacy and spaciousness.
Color acts as an emotional, physical and physiological stimulant, with warm colors feeling arousing/exciting and cool colors feeling calming.
Brightness influences the perception of spaciousness, with bright spaces feeling more spacious.
The context of activity (active vs. inactive) modulates the emotional perception of space, particularly intimacy and warmth, suggesting an embodied or task-dependent influence on affective responses.
implementation_implications: Architects and interior designers can use VR as a viable evaluation platform for new architectural concepts, allowing variable design parameters to create experiential spaces with emotional qualities.

Design principles for living spaces can be formulated based on correlations between design parameters (color, brightness, texture) and psychophysiological spatial aspects (warmth, coolness, excitement, calmness, intimacy, spaciousness, comfort, rest, work).
To create warmer or more exciting spaces, use warmer shades of warm colors (red, orange, yellow) and decrease brightness if the existing color is warm. For active occupants, decrease brightness.

To create cooler or calmer spaces, use cooler shades of cool colors (blue, green, purple) and increase brightness if the existing color is warm to make it cooler. For active occupants, increase brightness.
To increase spaciousness, increase brightness. To increase intimacy, decrease brightness.
For working environments, in dark settings, smooth texture is preferred over rough texture.

tables.description: Between-subjects design of the user study, showing experimental conditions, activity, number of participants, and male/female ratio.
Composition of the eight virtual test spaces based on combinations of color, brightness, and texture parameters.
Correlations between user's desired spatial qualities and corresponding design principles, outlining how to modify color and brightness for specific affective aspects.

limitations: The study used a CAVE-type display, which, while immersive, is still a simulated environment and may not fully replicate real-world sensory experiences.
The study focused on a single, square living space, limiting generalizability to other architectural forms or scales.
Only two colors (orange and blue) and two levels of brightness and texture were used, which is a simplification of the full spectrum of design possibilities.
The definition of 'intimate' might have been interpreted broadly by participants, not strictly as the opposite of 'spaciousness'.
The study did not explore the psychological and metaphysical dimensions of natural light, materiality, color, and texture in space-making beyond visual perception.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Environmental stimuli evoke emotional responses that can be described along dimensions of Pleasure, Arousal, and Dominance.
Specific colors (e.g., orange, blue) are associated with distinct emotional and perceptual qualities (e.g., warmth, coolness).
Specific shapes (e.g., round, angular) are associated with distinct emotional and perceptual qualities (e.g., comfort, tension).
